newsitem.title: USA: Consumer prices move up 0.3 percent in September.
newsitem.headline: Consumer prices move up 0.3 percent in September.

text.p: Consumer prices rose moderately in September, the Labour Department said Wednesday, new evidence that inflation remained under control despite the prolonged economic expansion.
The department said the Consumer Price Index rose 0.3 percent last month, following an increase of 0.1 percent in August.
The so-called core rate, excluding the usually volatile food and energy components, also rose 0.3 percent after rising 0.1 percent in August, the department said.
The September report matched Wall Street estimates of an increase of 0.3 percent for both the overall and core rate.
The new data also set the size of the annual cost of living increase for some 44 million Social Security recipients, who will see a 2.9 percent rise in their monthly payments take affect Jan 3.
"When you look at the details, everything came in as expected," said Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Government Securities Inc. "All of these things were expected. There's really no surprise."
The CPI report follows last week's Producer Price Index showing wholesale prices advanced modestly in September.

The price figures have been closely watched by the inflation-sensitive bond market and the high-flying stock market. This week the Dow Jones industrial average, the most widely watched stock market index, closed above 6,000 points for the first time. In afternoon trading Wednesday, the Dow was off 22 points at 5,982 on profit-taking.

Despite the moderate rise in September consumer prices, the benchmark U.S. Treasury bond fell 18/32 of a point, or $5.625 per $1,000 face value, and its yield climbed to 6.89 percent from 6.84 percent Tuesday.
Economists have become increasingly concerned that rising labour costs in a tightening job market could lead to a pickup in inflation in the months ahead.
In a separate but related report, the department said average weekly earnings of U.S. workers, after adjusting for inflation and seasonal factors, rose 0.8 percent in September.
The September increase followed a revised 1.2 percent gain in August real average weekly earnings. Previously, the department reported that August real earnings rose 0.7 percent.
But the CPI data suggested that so far, businesses have been cautious about passing along higher labour costs in the form of large price increases.
"These data are further confirmation that the recent acceleration in wage costs have not filtered through to the general price structure," said Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
Some analysts were more cautious.
"While inflation remains at bay, the risks cannot be eliminated by this morning's number," said Oscar Gonzalez of John Hancock Financial Services.

He noted that unemployment was very low and that the economy was moving faster than its long-term trend, adding that on its face at least, a 0.3 percent increase in the CPI hardly represented the death of inflation.
The department said food and beverage prices rose 0.5 percent following an increase of 0.3 percent in August as declines in vegetable prices were offset by increases in fruit and meat costs.

Housing prices edged up only 0.2 percent in the month, identical with the rise that occurred in August. Energy prices were unchanged following a decline of 0.6 percent in August, with gasoline prices down 0.4 percent in September.
New vehicle prices jumped 0.6 percent, posting the biggest rise since January 1991, when they were up an identical amount.

Analysts said while the vehicle price rise bore watching to see if it continued to escalate in October, it might reflect less discounting than usual on old model, 1996 cars rather than big jumps in prices for new, 1997 models.
At the same time, the department noted that 10 percent of the index reflected the 1997 models, a larger share than is usually included this early in the model year.
Apparel and its upkeep rose 0.5 percent after being down 1.4 percent in the prior month, an increase that had been anticipated considering the August decline.
Airline fares jumped 2.9 percent, but analysts said that reflected the reinstatement of fare taxes, a one-time event.
Overall transportation costs rose 0.5 percent after being down 0.2 percent. Medical care costs continued a pattern of modest increases, rising 0.2 percent to match the August figure.
